name: The Changelog
subtitle: Software Development, Open Source
audience: Software engineers, open source contributors, engineering leaders
why_good_fit: One of the most respected dev podcasts. Covers AI-native tooling, outbound sales infra, and open source projects. A guest spot here signals serious technical credibility.
how_to_pitch: Submit a guest request at changelog.com/request/podcast. They also accept news submissions at changelog.com/news/submit. Email: editors@changelog.com
pitch_tips: Come with a specific open source angle or a tool that solves a real engineering problem. They favor founders who also ship code.

name: Syntax
subtitle: Tasty Treats for Web Developers
audience: Full-stack and frontend developers, ~300K listeners
why_good_fit: Massive developer audience. Their 'Supper Club' format is perfect for founders of dev tools — one-on-one interview with a product maker.
how_to_pitch: Visit syntax.fm/guests or reach out on Twitter/X @syntaxfm. They are most responsive to DMs from people with a clear product story.
pitch_tips: Pitch the 'Supper Club' format specifically. Lead with what the tool does in one sentence and why developers love it.

name: Software Engineering Daily
subtitle: Daily technical interviews on software topics
audience: Senior software engineers, engineering managers, CTOs
why_good_fit: The most prolific dev podcast. Produces 5 episodes/week — high volume means they're always looking for guests with interesting tools or engineering stories.
how_to_pitch: Apply at softwareengineeringdaily.com/applying-to-host or contact via softwareengineeringdaily.com/contact. They also accept written pieces at softwareengineeringdaily.com/write
pitch_tips: They value technical depth. Come with a specific architecture decision, trade-off, or engineering challenge your product solves — not a product pitch.

name: JS Party
subtitle: A weekly celebration of JavaScript and the web
audience: JavaScript and web developers
why_good_fit: Part of the Changelog network. A guest spot on JS Party typically leads to being featured on Changelog's newsletter as well, multiplying reach.
how_to_pitch: Email editors@changelog.com or submit at changelog.com/request/podcast. Reference JS Party specifically.
pitch_tips: Best for founders of JavaScript-adjacent tools — bundlers, linters, frameworks, or AI copilots for web devs.

name: Ship It!
subtitle: Practical software delivery and DevOps
audience: Platform engineers, DevOps engineers, SREs
why_good_fit: Niche but highly engaged DevOps audience. Perfect if the tool touches deployment, automation, or developer workflow automation.
how_to_pitch: Email editors@changelog.com or DM @gerhardlazu on Twitter.
pitch_tips: Gerhard loves real production war stories. Lead with a specific incident or outage your tooling helped prevent.

name: CoRecursive
subtitle: Coding Stories
audience: Experienced software developers who love long-form storytelling
why_good_fit: Adam digs into the 'story behind the tool' — origin stories, failures, pivots. Ideal for a founder with an interesting technical backstory.
how_to_pitch: Email adam@corecursive.com. Keep the pitch short; lead with the story angle, not the product.
pitch_tips: Adam is specifically interested in human stories about building software — not product demos. Frame your pitch as a story about a problem you couldn't stop thinking about.

name: Developer Tea
subtitle: Short episodes for developers with intention
audience: Software developers focused on career growth
why_good_fit: Jonathan often invites founders building tools that improve developer productivity and mental overhead. Strong community angle.
how_to_pitch: Contact via developertea.com or Twitter @jcutrell.
pitch_tips: Frame the pitch around what your tool teaches developers or how it changes their workflow mindset — Jonathan is more interested in the 'why' than the 'what'.

name: Indie Hackers Podcast
subtitle: Building profitable online businesses
audience: Developer-founders, indie hackers, bootstrappers
why_good_fit: Huge audience of developer-founders who are the exact target persona for a dev tool. Great for sharing MRR milestones, growth tactics, and founding story.
how_to_pitch: Submit at indiehackers.com/podcast or DM @csallen on Twitter. Share revenue milestones and growth story upfront.
pitch_tips: They want concrete numbers — MRR, churn rate, CAC. Being transparent about what's working and what isn't is more compelling than a polished success story.

name: Talk Python To Me
subtitle: Python and related technologies
audience: Python developers across all skill levels
why_good_fit: If the product has a Python SDK, CLI, or heavy Python usage, this is the perfect placement. Michael's audience is deeply engaged and buying.
how_to_pitch: Email michael@talkpython.fm. Michael is responsive and appreciates direct, brief pitches with a clear Python angle.
pitch_tips: Must have a genuine Python story. Share a GitHub repo, pip package, or notebook integration. Michael does his homework before every interview.

name: Front End Happy Hour
subtitle: Conversations with engineers from top tech companies
hosts: Engineers from Netflix, Twitch, Atlassian, LinkedIn
audience: Frontend and full-stack engineers at mid-to-large companies
why_good_fit: The panel format with senior engineers at top companies gives product endorsement weight. Being featured signals adoption at scale.
how_to_pitch: Contact via frontendhappyhour.com or Twitter @FEHappyHour.
pitch_tips: The panel loves real-world performance metrics and engineering tradeoffs. Bring benchmarks, before/after DX data, or a story about scale.

name: Hanselminutes
subtitle: Fresh Air for Developers
audience: Broad developer audience, strong Microsoft/web developer overlap
why_good_fit: Scott is a VP at Microsoft and one of the most connected voices in developer tooling. A guest spot creates instant developer-community credibility.
how_to_pitch: Contact via hanselminutes.com/contact or Twitter @shanselman.
pitch_tips: Scott appreciates clear storytelling and has a radar for genuinely useful tools vs. hype. Lead with the developer problem you solve, not the AI angle.

name: The TWIML AI Podcast
subtitle: This Week in Machine Learning & AI
audience: ML engineers, AI researchers, data scientists
why_good_fit: Top-tier AI podcast. Guest list is a who's who of AI builders. Being on TWIML signals serious technical credibility in the AI space.
how_to_pitch: Pitch via twimlai.com/contact or sam@twimlai.com.
pitch_tips: Sam values technical depth and novel research angles. If the tool has an interesting ML architecture or uses LLMs in a non-obvious way, that's your hook.

name: Lenny's Podcast
subtitle: Product, growth, and career advice for builders
audience: Product managers, founders, and GTM leaders at SaaS companies
why_good_fit: Enormous audience of SaaS buyers and decision-makers. Lenny increasingly covers AI-native tools and founder stories. High reach among technical PMs who champion devtools.
how_to_pitch: Email lenny@lennyspodcast.com or submit via lennyspodcast.com. Lenny's team receives hundreds of pitches — a warm intro from a mutual connection is ideal.
pitch_tips: Lead with a contrarian insight or uncommon framework you've developed building the product. Lenny's audience wants something actionable they haven't heard before.

name: Software Engineering Radio
subtitle: The podcast for professional software developers
hosts: Rotating panel of volunteer IEEE engineers
audience: Mid-to-senior professional software engineers
why_good_fit: IEEE-backed with credibility in enterprise and mid-market software teams. Good for reaching engineers with budget authority in larger organizations.
how_to_pitch: Submit via se-radio.net/contact. They accept volunteer hosts and guest suggestions through their editorial process.
pitch_tips: Position the pitch around a software engineering best practice or pattern your tool enforces. Academic framing resonates well with this audience.

name: Fireship
subtitle: Fast-paced developer content, frameworks and AI
audience: Developers of all levels who want fast, dense content
why_good_fit: Fireship's '100 Seconds' and 'The Code Report' formats are cultural touchstones in the dev community. A feature or mention here can go viral overnight.
how_to_pitch: No public guest process. Best approach is Twitter/X DM @Fireship_dev or email via fireship.io. Sponsorships are available via fireship.io/sponsor.
pitch_tips: Jeff is drawn to tools with impressive demos — something visual, fast, or surprising. Build a 2-minute 'wow' demo before reaching out. He values brevity above all.

name: ThePrimeagen
subtitle: Raw takes on software engineering, tools, and culture
audience: Experienced software engineers who care deeply about developer ergonomics
why_good_fit: PrimeTime reacts to dev tool announcements in real-time — if the tool is interesting, he might cover it organically. His audience is highly opinionated and influential.
how_to_pitch: DM on Twitter @ThePrimeagen or Twitch. He occasionally has guests on his Twitch stream and ThePrimeagen channel. A genuinely interesting tool is the best pitch.
pitch_tips: Don't oversell. Prime's audience hates hype. Come with honest tradeoffs, a GitHub repo, and a real engineering problem. He respects technical honesty over polish.

name: Theo - t3.gg
subtitle: Hot takes on the JavaScript and TypeScript ecosystem
audience: Full-stack TypeScript/JavaScript developers and indie SaaS builders
why_good_fit: Theo is a major opinion leader in the TypeScript ecosystem. His audience overlaps heavily with early adopters of new developer tools.
how_to_pitch: Twitter @t3dotgg or Discord discord.gg/theo. He frequently collaborates with tool makers on demos and Q&A streams.
pitch_tips: Theo is attracted to tools with a strong TypeScript-first DX or tools that make an interesting architectural bet. He dislikes 'enterprise' framing — keep it developer-first.

name: TechWithTim
subtitle: Python, AI/ML, and software tutorials
audience: Students and junior to mid-level developers learning Python and AI
why_good_fit: Massive Python and AI audience. Tim regularly features tools and libraries in tutorial format — one tutorial video can drive thousands of signups.
how_to_pitch: Contact via techwithtim.net/contact or Twitter @TechWithTimm. Sponsorship and collab requests are handled through the site.
pitch_tips: Tim's audience responds best to tools they can try immediately. Offer a free tier and a step-by-step 'getting started' video script — Tim can turn that into a tutorial fast.

name: Fireship — CodeTV (Jason Lengstorf)
subtitle: Web dev challenge shows and tutorials
audience: Frontend and full-stack web developers
why_good_fit: Jason's 'Learn With Jason' format is specifically designed to showcase tools by having guests demo them live. A natural fit for any product with a compelling live demo.
how_to_pitch: Schedule directly at jason.energy/guest or DM @jlengstorf on Twitter.
pitch_tips: Jason's format requires you to teach something in ~90 minutes. Come with a clear 'what the viewer will build by the end' outcome. The more hands-on the better.

name: Forrest Knight
subtitle: Software architecture, AI tools, career content
audience: Mid to senior software engineers focused on architecture and career growth
why_good_fit: Forrest covers emerging dev tools and AI from a senior engineer's perspective. His audience has purchasing power and actively evaluates new tools.
how_to_pitch: Twitter @ForrestKnight or email via forrestknight.com.
pitch_tips: Position the tool as something that changes how senior engineers think about a problem, not just a beginner shortcut. Architecture and scalability angles land well.

name: Matt Pocock
subtitle: TypeScript educator and tool builder
audience: TypeScript developers ranging from intermediate to expert
why_good_fit: Matt is the leading TypeScript educator on YouTube. If the product has a TypeScript SDK or strong type safety story, Matt's audience will love it.
how_to_pitch: Twitter @mattpocockuk or Discord via Total TypeScript. Matt occasionally features tools that have interesting TypeScript integrations.
pitch_tips: Lead with the TypeScript angle — show the types, the inference, the DX. If there's a clever generic type in the codebase, that's your foot in the door.

name: Hussein Nasser
subtitle: Backend engineering, databases, and systems
audience: Backend and infrastructure engineers who want deep technical content
why_good_fit: Hussein covers backend tools and infrastructure at a deep technical level. His audience is highly influential in evaluating tools for production use.
how_to_pitch: Twitter @hnasr or DM on YouTube. Hussein occasionally covers tools that have a compelling systems story.
pitch_tips: Go deep on the technical underpinnings — what protocol does it use, how does it scale, what are the edge cases. This audience will dismiss anything shallow.

name: Draft.dev
subtitle: Technical content agency for developer tools
audience: DevRel teams and developer tool companies (via their published content on Hacker News, dev.to, etc.)
estimated_reach: Content placed in front of millions of developers via client blogs
why_good_fit: Draft.dev works with nearly every top dev tool company to produce technical tutorials and articles. Getting featured as a use case or subject in their content exposes the product to a huge developer audience.
how_to_pitch: Email hello@draft.dev or visit draft.dev/contact. Also worth pitching to be featured as a case study in their 'Learn' content hub.
pitch_tips: Draft.dev is a content agency — the best pitch is to propose a technical tutorial topic that uses the product and would genuinely help developers.

name: Changelog Weekly
subtitle: Weekly dev news email read by 50K+ devs
audience: Software engineers and open source contributors
why_good_fit: A single mention in Changelog Weekly can drive thousands of GitHub stars or signups overnight. It's the Hacker News of curated dev newsletters.
how_to_pitch: Submit news at changelog.com/news/submit. Include a clear one-liner about what the tool does and a GitHub repo or demo link.
pitch_tips: Open source tools or tools with a free tier get picked up most often. Include concrete metrics if available (GitHub stars, downloads, companies using it).

name: Bytes (bytes.dev)
subtitle: Your weekly JavaScript newsletter
audience: JavaScript developers — ~200K subscribers
why_good_fit: The most entertaining dev newsletter in the JS ecosystem. A mention feels organic and is actually read — open rates are extremely high for a newsletter this size.
how_to_pitch: Sponsorships and features at bytes.dev/sponsor. Also possible to submit via Twitter @uidotdev.
pitch_tips: Bytes has a distinct humor-first voice. The best features are tools with a fun angle or a genuinely surprising capability. Dry enterprise tools don't get organic mentions.
